name: Adam Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I help a school brass group on Wednesdays, teach beginners at the community hall and edit small studio recordings when asked. I left after secondary school, and I still ask more experienced players to check my charts; the children like it when I play a wrong note and fix it with them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that work mean for home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rosa works in park maintenance, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. The pay is typical for a musician, we've saved about three months of expenses, and there are some other school music jobs nearby.

I'd welcome **tidier reminders** if they help pupils arrive ready to play.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and Rosa's wages absorb one moved studio date.
I still need the **school timetable** before promising another room.
do: Keep the **Wednesday school group** and Friday hall sessions this term.
Save **fifty per studio date** after travel and children's bills are paid.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about moved sessions, with the next mortgage payment covered.

fieldNote: His **three-month cushion** and partner's wage absorb a single delayed recording fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the brass players a tidier schedule helps, but it doesn't put air through a trumpet. The school ensemble still needs a patient adult to help children find the first note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI sometimes to sort lesson reminders after a colleague shows me a reliable tool. We have about three months of expenses saved, and Rosa's park maintenance wage is steady; a missed recording date would be annoying, not a mortgage emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the Wednesday school brass group and my Friday community hall practice sessions this term. If the little studio pays its two monthly recording dates, I'll put fifty from each fee into the house reserve after travel and the children's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about dates moving, but the school group and Rosa's pay keep the next mortgage payment covered. I can afford to let one studio date slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the delayed studio date affect the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A jingle session moved in March, and the studio paid it in April. I used the school group's fee for the gas bill and didn't need savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must be settled before you take another hall date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the school's next term timetable with the teacher before promising Friday practice to a different hall. The pupils need a room more than I need a clever calendar. A calendar can find a room; it cannot fill a trumpet.

I'd keep **children's recordings** out of unapproved tools.
think: **Arranging and edits** bring about a quarter of my income and may shrink.
A cheaper **score check** does not replace the money lost from fewer paid hours.
do: Bring **prep-hour invoices** to the musicians association this month.
Trial a colleague-tested **AI checker** on my own score after licence and note checks; stop if pupil audio is required.
Ask for **two paid prep hours** per group session before agreeing to new terms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a quarter of pay and the mortgage reserve.
S1.quote: A saved hour is not a paid hour.
fieldNote: He makes a **specific paid-hours request** rather than treating AI savings as wages.
His **tool trial** uses owned material, a checked licence and note-by-note review, never pupil audio.

steps.text: Take paid prep-hour invoices to musicians association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the school teacher that generated parts may be useful, but children must know who made the recording they hear. I would ask the musicians association to press for paid preparation hours when the school changes its timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My simple arrangements and recording edits bring about a quarter of my pay. Those can be cheap software jobs soon, while the brass group probably keeps its room; losing the fees would eat our reserve one mortgage month at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll list the paid prep hours on my school invoice and take them to the association's next meeting. In the first year of the change, I'll trial the AI score checker a colleague uses on my own old arrangement, but only after checking its licence and comparing each note with the paper copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a quarter of my pay. I can learn a tested tool, but the school may still cut preparation pay. A saved hour is not a paid hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What material would you keep out of the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not upload a child's rehearsal recording to the checker. If it needs a live file, I would stop the trial and ask the school what consent it has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exact preparation minimum would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the school for a written minimum of two paid preparation hours per group session. If it refuses, I would keep the existing class while asking another nearby school what it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the school that 2028 is too close to leave paid hours vague. I would keep playing the community hall sessions while people still turn up for live brass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI in 2028 could prepare parts, edit demos and plan beginner lessons for less than I can. Robot players arrive about 2031, but my screen fees could vanish before then; three months saved and Rosa's wage would not cover a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the school for next year's paid timetable and separate school, studio and hall fees. In the first year after 2028, if studio edits halve, I'll apply for an advertised brass post only if my schooling qualifies, its hours fit the children, and net pay after travel replaces the lost edit fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, edging toward alarm if the school cuts too. I can try other posts, but applications take time. A job application isn't money for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there school posts open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two schools sometimes advertise music aides, but I have not seen a vacancy this term. I'd ask for the actual pay scale and whether my secondary-school education is enough before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the Wednesday group also goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the school also cuts the Wednesday group, I would ask the lender about a temporary payment change before falling behind. I'd get the total interest in writing and discuss it with Rosa first.

I'd ask staff to see the **music budget** before new contracts are signed.

Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the hall players five years lets us build paid group lessons without pretending the software will wait. I would ask the school to share any new music budget with staff before it signs contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could replace my arrangements and routine lesson planning; robots would reach hands-on playing about 2034. Five years gives me time to improve my teaching and ask for stronger school hours, though cheap tools may cut edits earlier.

transcript.text: Next term I'll ask the school to let me run a six-week beginner brass circle with a written fee and no extra room charge. If eight pupils pay and the school confirms my hours, I'll repeat it; in the first year after 2031, I'll keep it only if eight families renew and my paid fee remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because those recording edits may fade before 2031. The circle is a test, not a second mortgage payment yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend on instruments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the school's instruments, not buy eight trumpets. If the school will not put the room and fee in writing, I'd keep my usual Wednesday group instead. I won't buy eight trumpets to find out whether eight children want a lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if only six pupils pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight paying families cover the accompanist and my teaching hour. If only six enrol, I would refund them and ask the school what they would support next term.

transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the brass group that a decade is enough time to teach a new row of children, but the hall still needs paying families now. I would ask the school for a durable paid place rather than a grand promise about music's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036 and robots may play around 2039. I cannot count on retirement, and studio editing may shrink well before then; I need school teaching and community performances that bring regular fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the school about a paid instrumental aide contract and check whether its required course has a grant. I'll apply only if another school posts paid hours, my education qualifies and the pay covers mortgage and travel; I will keep Wednesday teaching until an offer is signed. By 2036 I'll aim to save six months of expenses from paid teaching and hall fees; in the first year after AGI, I'll keep an aide role only if paid hours renew and net pay covers travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about paying for training while the school merely talks about an aide post. Three months saved and Rosa's pay let us test a funded course without borrowing. A decade doesn't sign the next school term for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a posted aide vacancy or just a conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school has talked about an aide position but has not posted one. I would enrol in the course only if the school accepts its certificate, a grant pays the fee, and Rosa can cover the evening childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave your Wednesday group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not give up the Wednesday group until another school signs a paid offer. If nothing opens, I'll keep the hall work and save what I can from booked dates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the studio edits may fall before I can secure another school post. A written school timetable, genuine vacancies and clear lender terms if the group is cut would help us plan without guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a school tool can use children's recordings. A child's recording needs family permission before any school tool touches it.

headlineQuote: A child's recording needs family permission before any school tool touches it.
portrait: Adam is a **43-year-old** junior musician with secondary education, teaching brass groups and editing small studio recordings.
He and Rosa have **two children**, a mortgage and three months saved, with some local school music jobs.
He uses **AI occasionally** after a colleague proves a tool, while fearing early losses in arrangement and editing fees.
He tests **school brass teaching** with written terms, eight paying pupils and no new instruments before shifting work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because studio editing fees could fall before another school post opens.
whatWouldHelp: A **written timetable**, real school vacancies and clear lender costs would help protect the mortgage.
